qualitative_or_quantitative_description.value: KAM shows an evident stress concentration at the precipitation location of the carbide and the Be–Fe phase; the distribution of these precipitates is primarily concentrated at the grain boundary and phase interface. In 1.5Be the stress-concentration distribution is relatively uniform.

interaction_type.value: crack nucleation and arrest in dual-phase structure

qualitative_or_quantitative_description.value: In 1.0Be and 1.5Be dual-phase steels, quasi-cleavage cracks initially occur and rapidly expand inside the grains of the brittle ferrite phase, and are immediately hindered when they expand to the adjacent austenite region with better plasticity; the Be–Fe phase accelerates crack propagation and reduces plasticity.

slip_behavior.value: Under the action of external force a large number of dislocation slip movements and accumulation occur inside the steel; dislocation density increases with Be content (Fig. 16), strengthening the steel. Austenite is destroyed after large plastic deformation.

phase_evolution.value: In the as-cast structure the Be–Fe phase has an 'ancient Chinese character' / needle-like morphology; after hot deformation (rolled 1.5Be) the needle-like compounds decrease evidently and point-like compounds increase, with the distribution changing from aggregate to dispersed; most Be is solubilised into the matrix. When remaining Be cannot dissolve in austenite it precipitates on ferrite as spot-like compounds.

interface_notes.value: EDS of the rolled 1.5Be austenite/ferrite junction shows the inner strip-shaped structure is Mn-rich and Al-rich (ferrite) and the outer strip-shaped structure is Mn-rich and Al-poor (austenite), i.e., the elongated structure is ferrite surrounded by austenite.

unmapped_findings: The rolled 1.5Be (Fe–30Mn–10Al–1.5C–1.5Be, hot-rolled at 1050 °C) alloy belongs to the dual-phase austenite (γ-Fe, FCC) + ferrite (α-Fe/δ, BCC) group; XRD of the rolled 1.5Be steel reports Be11Fe, Be12Fe, Be2Fe and Be2C peaks (b0036), while Fig. 7 legend keys only Be11Fe and Be2Fe.
Density discrepancy for 1.5Be: the abstract quotes ~6.25 g/cm³ (b0009) while Table 3 (rolled state) gives 6.29 ±0.05 g/cm³ (b0065); b0099 also states 6.29 g/cm³.

DSC peak discrepancy: b0035 quotes a Be-free steel transformation temperature of 1278.8 °C, whereas the Fig. 6 label for 0Be reads 1320 °C (broad peak rising from ~1270 °C). For 1.5Be the printed peak is 1154.8 °C.

The as-cast microhardness Table 2 (Fig. 5) values (0Be/0.5Be/1.0Be/1.5Be austenite 453.31–479.74 HV; ferrite 437.40–452.54 HV; Be–Fe phase 483.50 and 477.16 HV) pertain to the AS-CAST state and NOT to this rolled sample, so they are excluded from the rolled 1.5Be property records.
The grain-size distribution of rolled 1.5Be (Fig. 14d) shows a single dominant bar in the 12–13 μm region (~0.30–0.32 area fraction), consistent with the ~13 μm reported in b0050.

Fracture of the rolled 1.5Be steel is a mixed ductile-dimple/cleavage (plastic-brittle) mode; spherical precipitates ~2 μm were observed at the bottom of dimples in high-Be steels, acting as micropore-crack nuclei (b0069).

The strength-ductility product (Ashby plot, Fig. 20) places the Be steels at the lowest density with a high product; the 0.5Be sample gives the highest strength-ductility product (above the 45 GPa% gridline).
